newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - SOUTH AFRICA'S SAVINGS - BY EDWARD OSBORN.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - SOUTH AFRICA'S SAVINGS - BY EDWARD OSBORN.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd
The favourite lament of bankers and central bankers is the low savings rate. The Victorian virtue of thrift is no longer with us.

The lamentation over low savings invariably arises in the context of investment, which to every one is obviously a good thing. There is an implicit suggestion that investment turns on the level of savings; the more savings the greater the volume of investment.

This, unfortunately, reflects that bankers are not economically literate, for the two are independent of each other, being carried out by different agents and with different motivations. Broadly, however, it is the level of investment activity that determines the rate of savings.

This is clear for a closed economy, for the greater the investment the higher the level of economic activity, disposable incomes and likely level of savings. The absence of savings, however, can be a drag on investment through its financing in that interest rates will be that much higher and investments sensitive to interest rates will be curbed. In the national accounts savings and investment are always equal, as they say, ex post.
In South Africa savings are now down to 16.7 percent of GDP, but this reflects the low level of investment activity, or fixed capital formation.

Savings are dominated by the corporate sector. In 1995, for example, total corporate savings in the form of depreciation provisions and company after-depreciation savings amounted to 94.2 billion rand, whereas the total net national savings amounted to 81 billion rand. The savings of the private household sector amounted to six billion rand, but there was a dissavings by the government sector of 19.2 billion rand.

Given this structure of savings the banker prescription for the improvement of the economy will be the reduction of government dissavings, or the budget deficit, and the encouragement of private household savings.

The budget deficit embraces both government dissavings, general government capital formation, capital transfers and loans. However, the major part is dissavings. The reduction of these dissavings through increased taxes would simply be a shift from the other sectors reducing their savings. Hence the usual course to follow would be through reduced government expenditures, actually non-interest expenditures.

If this can be done through the elimination of waste and inefficiency, well and good, but if it is to be achieved through sharp reductions in the size of the bureaucracy care has to be taken for the measures can be deflationary, resulting in a drop in GDP and indeed in savings.

The intended sharp drop in the budget deficit to four percent next year is probably more hubris than practical but if it were to be achieved through draconian cut-backs the effects could be serious indeed, coming on top of the general tendency of recent years of downsizing of establishments.

Which brings us to the matter of the personal sector savings. These have been in decline in recent years and this has been the subject of much head shaking and consternation. The prescription is more voluntary savings and less consumption expenditure. This needs a little more teasing out.

First, the sector's savings are derived in the national accouts as the residual or difference between estimated disposable income after payment of direct taxes and estimated private consumption expenditure. Clearly, savings as a residual are a net aggregate. Gross institutional savings in the form of pension contributions and life policy premiums of about 50 billion rand are reduced to a net savings figure for the sector of six billion rand.

Significantly consumption expenditure has been rising as a proportion of disposable income over the last three years of the economic upturn, from 94.6 percent in 1993 to 97.6 percent in 1995. Consumption expenditure has thus been rising relatively and this has been financed in a number of ways.

Unfortunately no official efforts have been made as yet to show the make up of the financing of consumption expenditure. But the financing would be in terms of the normal categories of disposable income, customer credit, credit card finance, hire purchase financing and other forms of bank loans and advances, and should embrace also the redistribution of income through crime and the diversion of income through boycotting.

Crime in the form of burglaries, car thefts and other theft that results in expenditure on the replacement of goods through the agency of short-term insurers will be an addition to private consumption expenditure and an effective reduction in savings. In effect such crime-based consumption is a redistribution of income through the mechanism of the insurance industry.

The stratum of consumption in respect of goods in replacement of stolen goods and property is considerable and would be contained in the total claims on the short-term insurers for motor and miscellaneous business, which were 5.6 billion rand in 1995. The Nedcor Project on Crime, Violence and Investment quite rightly gives emphasis to the cost of crime in South Africa.
The other side of the coin, however, is the dependence of the South African economy on crime in terms of sustaining consumption expenditure and the production that is its counterpart.

For example, according to the Nedcor study there were 97,950 car thefts in 1995, that is nearly 47 percent of total sales in the year. Obviously not all these car thefts resulted in new car replacements, but a significant proportion would be.

Boycotting of rents and local government rates and other charges has also bolstered purchasing power, impacting on total consumption expenditure and the financial balances of other sectors, in particular worsening the deficit position of the government sector. Boycotting represents a diversion of the disposal of income to the disadvantage of government, in particular, but to the advantage of the sectors producing consumer goods, say.

Finally one has to take note of the apparent paradox that investment decisions are more likely to be influenced by growing consumption rather than by growing savings. The Nedcor project has demonstrated quite clearly that the major motivations for fixed investment lie with economic growth and market opportunities. Both of these are strongly dictated by market opportunities. Both of these are strongly dictated by the level of private consumption expenditure, rather than the attenuation of consumption in favour of savings.

Regrettably crime and boycotting have made a positive contribution towards sustaining economic growth in South Africa and, indeed, there is a fair degree of dependence of the economy on anti-social behaviour. Not that it is to be encouraged. It just happens to be a fact of life.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
